title: How to Make a Family Screen Covenant
excerpt: Screens are not neutral. They form your children whether or not you decide they should. A covenant is how a family decides on purpose instead of drifting by default.
body:
Most families do not choose their relationship with screens. They drift into it. A device is handed over to keep a toddler quiet, a phone is bought because everyone else has one, and one ordinary decision at a time, the screen moves to the center of the home and no one ever voted on it. By the time a parent notices, the habits are set and the fight is uphill.

The alternative is not a list of bans barked from above. It is a covenant. A covenant is a promise the household makes together, with reasons attached, that everyone including the parents agrees to keep. It works where rules fail because it treats the family as a body deciding how it wants to live, not a warden managing inmates.

## Why screens are a discipleship question

We imagine technology is neutral, a mere tool that does what we point it at. It is not. The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt has spent years documenting what the smartphone did to a generation of children, and the picture is grim: rising anxiety, collapsing attention, a childhood spent looking down. The devices are engineered to capture, designed by people whose income depends on your child's inability to look away.

This is not a side issue to family discipleship. It is central. The screen is forming your children's loves, their attention, their sense of what is real and what matters, every hour they hold it. The only question is whether that formation happens by your design or by a stranger's. A family screen covenant is how you take that decision back.

## Make it together, and write it down

Gather the whole family, old enough to talk, and make it a real conversation, not a sentencing. Ask what screens are for in your home and what they cost. Let the children speak. They often know more about the cost than you expect, because they feel it. Then write the covenant down, plainly, where everyone can see it.

A good covenant names a few clear things. When screens are on and when they are off. Where they live, and where they do not, because the bedroom at night is where most of the damage is done. What they are for, and what they are not. And crucially, what the family will do instead, because a vacuum gets filled, and an hour taken from screens must be given to something.

## The parents are under it too

Here is the line most family screen rules cross, and the reason they fail. The parents exempt themselves. They take the phone from the child while never looking up from their own. Children are not fooled and they are not formed by words; they are formed by what they watch you do. A covenant that does not bind the parents is not a covenant. It is hypocrisy with a chore chart.

So put yourself under it. No phones at the table means yours too. Devices out of the bedroom means yours too. This is the hard part, and it is the whole part. I have lectured a child about screen time with a phone in my own hand, and the lecture was worth exactly nothing, and I knew it. The most powerful thing you can do for your children's relationship with their devices is to fix your own.

## Name what you are protecting

A covenant of bare prohibition feels like loss, and children resist loss. So name the thing you are guarding. "We keep screens out of the bedroom so the last and first thoughts of the day are not a stranger's. We turn them off at dinner so we can see each other's faces. We do this because you are worth more than what the screen wants from you." Frame every limit as a fence around a treasure, because that is what it is.

## Expect to fail and renegotiate

The covenant will be broken, by the children and by you. That is not the end of it. A covenant is meant to be returned to, confessed against, and renewed. Sit down again. Adjust what is not working. Hold the line on what matters. The goal is not a perfect record. It is a family that keeps choosing on purpose instead of drifting by default.

## This week

Gather the family this week for one honest conversation about screens. Ask what they are for and what they cost you. Together, decide three things: when screens are off, where they do not go, and what you will do instead. Write it on something and put it where you eat. Then put yourself under it first, harder than anyone, because they are watching you more than they are listening to you.

What you protect now in your children's attention, you will not have to fight to recover later. And what you surrender now, you may not get back.
